are small and the creations of his mind and art pass away,
when thus his pride and boasting fade-then there comes to
him a sense of his smallness, a sense of humility, but also at
the same time a feeling of release and redemption. It spells
release for man not only when he feels his anxieties dissipated
but also when the pressure of responsibility slackens. He feels
emancipated when control is taken out of his own hands and
he knows himself to be sustained by a mightier hand, when
he no longer needs to give his life its law, but knows himselt
to be subject to a greater law, which relieves him of ultimate
care and responsibility, when he becomes aware that his lite
too is governed by the divine ordinance: "While the earth
remains..." And it is just this feeling of release through
being controlled and enclasped by an infinite power, which
man experiences-even if only momentarily—when he opens
his heart to the subduing beauty of nature. For the infinite
power which is here perceptible to him in sensuous embodi-
ment—can he call it anything else but God? And further, it
is no accident that the human imagination, when it delights
to picture to itself the bliss which surrounds the Deity, repre-
sents paradise as a gloriously beautiful garden.
Hence does not man speak with justice about God meeting
him in the world of nature? Certainly, it is with justice that
he speaks thus, and in fact with far greater justice than he
himself realizes. And precisely because he does not himself
know with what justification he can speak thus, his argument
is at bottom unjustified. Why and to what extent is it
unjustified?
III
"While the earth remains ..." Let us not forget the
beginning of this text: "While, so long as ...", which implies
that the earth will not last for ever and that neither has it
eternally existed. In such a word it is affirmed that the world
and nature is God's creation, and that over this created
world stands the Creator and His sovereign will which is not
